tool.name: Node.js
tool.tagline: JavaScript runtime for servers, CLIs and tooling, built on V8 and libuv
tool.description: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, pairing Google's V8 engine with an event loop and non-blocking I/O. It powers web servers and APIs, command-line tools, build systems and real-time services, and its npm ecosystem is the largest package registry in the world. Learning Node lets you use one language across the whole web stack.

concepts.name: What Node.js is
concepts.summary: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser on V8, with an event loop and built-in modules for files, network and processes.
concepts.why: Knowing what Node is (and isn't) tells you what code will run in it and why its I/O model looks the way it does.
concepts.body:
**Node.js** is a JavaScript runtime: it takes Google's **V8** engine (the same one in Chrome) and wraps it in a C++ program that adds what a browser doesn't give you — reading files, opening sockets, spawning processes, reading environment variables. That glue is mostly provided by **libuv**, a library that handles asynchronous I/O and the **event loop**.

The language is the same JavaScript you know. What changes is the environment:

- There is no `window`, no `document`, no DOM. Instead you get `process`, `Buffer`, and built-in modules such as `node:fs`, `node:http` and `node:path`.
- Many web APIs exist anyway: `fetch`, `URL`, `AbortController`, `setTimeout`, `structuredClone`, `TextEncoder`, `crypto.randomUUID()`, web streams and `WebSocket` are all global.
- Your program is a long-lived process you control, not a page the user opens.

Node's defining design choice is **non-blocking I/O on a single JavaScript thread**. When you read a file or wait for an HTTP response, Node hands the work to the operating system (or libuv's thread pool) and keeps running other JavaScript. When the result is ready, your callback or `await` resumes. One process can therefore juggle thousands of concurrent connections without a thread per request — which is why Node is popular for web servers, APIs, CLIs, build tools and real-time apps.

The flip side: CPU-heavy JavaScript blocks everything else on that thread. Node is great at waiting on many things at once, less so at crunching numbers in JS (workers help there).

This course targets **Node.js 22 LTS**. Even-numbered releases become Long-Term Support and are what you should run in production; check yours with `node --version`.
takeaways: Node = V8 + libuv + built-in modules, no DOM
I/O is non-blocking; one JS thread serves many concurrent operations
CPU-heavy JavaScript blocks everything on that thread
Use an even-numbered LTS release (22) in production
pitfalls: Expecting browser objects like `window` or `document` to exist.

quiz.q: Why can a single Node process serve thousands of slow HTTP clients at once?
options: It creates one OS thread per connection
V8 compiles each request to native code in parallel
I/O waits don't block the JavaScript thread; results are handled as events
Node runs every request in a separate worker process
quiz.explain: Node delegates waiting to the OS/libuv and runs other JavaScript meanwhile, so idle connections cost almost nothing.

concepts.name: Running scripts, the REPL and --watch
concepts.summary: Run files with node, experiment in the REPL, evaluate one-liners and restart automatically on save with --watch.
concepts.why: These are the commands you use every day while writing and debugging Node code.
concepts.body:
The simplest way to run code is `node app.js`. Node executes the file top to bottom, then keeps the process alive as long as there is pending work — an open server, a timer, an unfinished read. When nothing is left, the process exits on its own.

Running `node` with no arguments opens the **REPL** (read–eval–print loop). It is ideal for poking at an API:

- `_` holds the last result; `.help` lists commands; `.editor` lets you paste multi-line code; `.exit` or Ctrl+D quits.
- Top-level `await` works, and built-in modules are preloaded: type `fs.` and press Tab.

For quick one-offs use `-e` (evaluate) or `-p` (evaluate and print):

```bash
node -p "os.cpus().length"
node -e "console.log(process.versions.v8)"
```

During development, `node --watch app.js` restarts the process whenever the file or anything it imports changes — no nodemon needed. Combine it with `--watch-path=./src` to watch a directory.

Useful companions:

- `node --run dev` runs the `dev` script from `package.json`, faster than `npm run` because it skips npm's startup.
- `node --check file.js` only parses the file, catching syntax errors.
- `node --env-file=.env app.js` loads environment variables (covered later).

Since 22.18 Node can also run TypeScript files directly by **stripping type annotations** (`node app.ts`); it does not type-check, so keep `tsc` in your workflow for that.

Finally, a Unix script can start with the shebang `#!/usr/bin/env node`; mark it executable (`chmod +x`) and it runs like any other command.
takeaways: `node file.js` runs a script; the process exits when no work is pending
The REPL supports top-level await and has built-in modules preloaded
`--watch` restarts on changes; `--run` runs package.json scripts quickly
pitfalls: Thinking `--watch` or type stripping type-checks or bundles code — they only restart and strip.

quiz.q: A script calls setInterval and nothing else. What happens when it reaches the last line?
options: The process stays alive because the interval is pending work
Node throws because the event loop is still busy
The interval runs once and the process exits
quiz.explain: Active timers (and servers, sockets, etc.) keep the event loop — and therefore the process — alive.

concepts.name: Modules: ES modules vs CommonJS
concepts.summary: Node supports ES modules (import/export) and the older CommonJS (require). Learn how Node picks one and how they interoperate.
concepts.why: Every Node file is one or the other, and mixing them wrongly is the most common source of confusing startup errors.
concepts.body:
Node has two module systems:

- **ES modules (ESM)** — the JavaScript standard: `import` / `export`, top-level `await`, imports are resolved before any code runs.
- **CommonJS (CJS)** — Node's original system: `require()` and `module.exports`, loaded synchronously at the moment `require` is called.

New code should be ESM. Node decides the format per file:

- `.mjs` is always ESM, `.cjs` always CommonJS.
- `.js` follows the nearest `package.json`: `"type": "module"` means ESM; no field (or `"commonjs"`) means CJS. Node 22 can also detect ESM syntax in an ambiguous `.js` file, but being explicit is better.

Import built-ins with the `node:` prefix — `import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises"` — so they can never be confused with an npm package of the same name.

ESM rules that trip people up:

- Relative imports need the **file extension**: `import { add } from "./math.js"`.
- `require`, `__dirname` and `__filename` don't exist. Use `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` (Node 20.11+), or `import.meta.url`.
- JSON needs an import attribute: `import data from "./data.json" with { type: "json" }`.

Interop: ESM can `import` a CommonJS module (its `module.exports` becomes the default export). Going the other way, Node 22.12+ lets `require()` load a synchronous ES module (one without top-level `await`); otherwise use dynamic `import()`, which works in both systems and returns a promise.

Prefer **named exports** for most things — they make refactoring and tree-shaking easier and show up in editor autocomplete.
takeaways: `"type": "module"` in package.json makes `.js` files ESM
Use `node:` for built-ins and include file extensions in relative imports
`import.meta.dirname` replaces `__dirname` in ESM
Dynamic `import()` works everywhere; `require(esm)` only for sync ESM
pitfalls: Writing `import x from './util'` without `.js` — ESM does not guess extensions.
Using `__dirname` in an ES module and getting a ReferenceError.

quiz.q: A package.json has no "type" field. How does Node treat app.js containing require() calls?
options: It refuses to run without a type field
quiz.explain: Without "type": "module", .js files default to CommonJS.

quiz.q: In an ES module, how do you get the directory of the current file?
quiz.explain: import.meta.dirname is the ESM equivalent; process.cwd() is where the process was started, which may differ.

concepts.name: npm and package.json
concepts.summary: Create a project with npm init, install packages, and understand what package.json records and what node_modules is.
concepts.why: Almost every Node project starts with package.json and depends on packages from the npm registry.
concepts.body:
**npm** ships with Node and does two jobs: it installs packages from the public registry, and it runs your project's scripts. A project is any folder with a **package.json**, created with `npm init -y`.

The fields you will touch most:

- `name`, `version` — identity, required if you publish.
- `type` — set to `"module"` for ES modules.
- `scripts` — named commands: `"dev": "node --watch src/server.js"`, `"test": "node --test"`. Run them with `npm run dev`; `npm test` and `npm start` are shortcuts.
- `dependencies` — packages your code needs at runtime.
- `devDependencies` — tools only needed while developing (test helpers, linters, TypeScript).
- `engines` — the Node versions you support, e.g. `">=22"`.

Installing:

```bash
npm install express          # adds to dependencies
npm install -D eslint        # adds to devDependencies
npm uninstall express
npx eslint .                 # run a package's binary without a global install
```

Packages land in **node_modules/**, a folder you never edit and never commit (add it to `.gitignore`). Node finds packages there by walking up from the importing file's directory.

Scripts run with `node_modules/.bin` on the `PATH`, so `"lint": "eslint ."` uses the locally installed eslint — no global installs needed, and every developer gets the same version.

Avoid `npm install -g` for project tools; keep them in `devDependencies` so the project describes everything it needs. Global installs are fine for personal utilities you use across projects.
concepts.code:
# Start a project and add a dependency
mkdir hello-api && cd hello-api
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm pkg set scripts.dev="node --watch server.js" scripts.test="node --test"
npm install express
npm install -D @types/node

# package.json now contains (abridged):
# {
#   "name": "hello-api",
#   "type": "module",
#   "scripts": { "dev": "node --watch server.js", "test": "node --test" },
#   "dependencies": { "express": "^5.1.0" },
#   "devDependencies": { "@types/node": "^22.10.0" }
# }

npm run dev        # or: node --run dev
npx eslint --version
takeaways: package.json describes the project: type, scripts, dependencies
`dependencies` for runtime, `devDependencies` for tooling
Never edit or commit node_modules; `npx` runs local binaries
pitfalls: Installing project tools globally so the project silently depends on your machine.

quiz.q: A test framework your code only uses during development should be installed with…
quiz.explain: -D records it under devDependencies, so production installs can skip it.

concepts.name: Versions, lockfiles and npm ci
concepts.summary: Read semver ranges like ^1.4.2, understand package-lock.json, and install reproducibly with npm ci.
concepts.why: Reproducible installs prevent "works on my machine" bugs and surprise breakages from transitive updates.
concepts.body:
npm packages use **semantic versioning**: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. A major bump may break you, a minor adds features compatibly, a patch only fixes bugs. In `package.json` you declare a **range**, not an exact version:

- `^1.4.2` — any `1.x.y` at or above 1.4.2 (the default npm writes). For `0.x` versions the caret is stricter: `^0.4.2` means `>=0.4.2 <0.5.0`.
- `~1.4.2` — patch updates only: `>=1.4.2 <1.5.0`.
- `1.4.2` — exactly that version.

Ranges alone would make every install potentially different, which is why npm writes **package-lock.json**. It records the exact version, download URL and integrity hash of *every* package in the tree, including dependencies of dependencies. Commit it.

Two install commands, two purposes:

- `npm install` — resolves ranges, may update the lockfile. Use it when adding or upgrading packages.
- `npm ci` — installs exactly what the lockfile says, deletes node_modules first, and fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree. Use it in CI and Docker builds.

To maintain dependencies:

- `npm outdated` lists packages with newer versions.
- `npm update` upgrades within your ranges; a major upgrade needs `npm install pkg@latest` and reading the changelog.
- `npm ls pkg` shows why a package is in your tree.
- `npm audit` reports known vulnerabilities.

Every dependency is code you run with full privileges. Prefer fewer, well-maintained packages, and check the weekly downloads and maintenance status before adding one.
concepts.code:
# package.json ranges
#   "express": "^5.1.0"   -> 5.1.0 up to (not including) 6.0.0
#   "zod":     "~3.24.1"  -> 3.24.x only
#   "uuid":    "11.0.3"   -> exactly 11.0.3

npm install            # resolve ranges, update package-lock.json if needed
git add package.json package-lock.json

# In CI / Dockerfile: exact, clean, fails on mismatch
npm ci

npm outdated           # what is behind?
npm install express@latest   # deliberate major upgrade
npm ls debug           # which packages pull in 'debug'?
npm audit              # known vulnerabilities
takeaways: `^` allows minor and patch updates, `~` only patches
Commit package-lock.json; it pins the whole dependency tree
Use `npm ci` for reproducible builds
pitfalls: Deleting package-lock.json to "fix" an install, which silently upgrades the whole tree.

quiz.q: package.json says "lib": "^2.3.0". Which version could npm install install?
quiz.explain: The caret allows any 2.x at or above 2.3.0, so 2.9.1 fits; 3.0.0 is a new major.

quiz.q: Why use npm ci rather than npm install in a CI pipeline?
options: It installs exactly the lockfile's versions and fails on mismatch
It is the only command that runs postinstall scripts
It upgrades packages to their latest versions
quiz.explain: npm ci gives a clean, reproducible install from the lockfile and errors if the lockfile is out of sync.

concepts.name: Reading and writing files with fs
concepts.summary: Use node:fs/promises to read, write, list and inspect files and directories with async/await.
concepts.why: Config files, uploads, logs, generated output — sooner or later every Node program touches the file system.
concepts.body:
The `node:fs` module offers three styles of the same operations: callbacks (`fs.readFile(path, cb)`), synchronous (`fs.readFileSync`) and promises. In application code use the promise API from **`node:fs/promises`** with `await`.

The everyday functions:

- `readFile(path, "utf8")` — whole file as a string (omit the encoding to get a `Buffer` of bytes).
- `writeFile(path, data)` — create or replace; `appendFile` adds to the end.
- `readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` — entries with `isFile()` / `isDirectory()`; add `recursive: true` to walk subfolders.
- `mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })` — creates parents and doesn't fail if it already exists.
- `stat(path)` — size, timestamps, type.
- `rm(path, { recursive: true, force: true })` — delete files or trees.
- `rename`, `copyFile`, `cp` (recursive copy), `access`.

Failures reject with an error whose `code` tells you what happened: `ENOENT` (no such file), `EACCES` (permission), `EEXIST`, `EISDIR`. Check `err.code` rather than the message text.

Don't call `access()` or `stat()` to check whether a file exists before opening it — another process can change things in between. Just attempt the operation and handle `ENOENT`.

Synchronous functions block the event loop for the whole operation. They are fine in a CLI script or at startup (loading config once) but never inside a request handler.

`readFile` loads everything into memory; for large files or files you process line by line, use streams (later lesson). Relative paths resolve against the process's **current working directory**, not the file's location — build absolute paths with `import.meta.dirname` (next lesson).
takeaways: Use `node:fs/promises` with await in application code
Handle errors by `err.code` (ENOENT, EACCES...), don't pre-check existence
Sync APIs block the event loop — only for scripts and startup
pitfalls: Using relative paths and being surprised when the script is run from another directory.
Reading huge files with readFile instead of streaming them.

quiz.q: You want to load settings.json but use defaults if it doesn't exist. What's the robust approach?
options: Call stat in a loop until the file appears
Call readFile and handle an error with code ENOENT
Use readFileSync inside a request handler
quiz.explain: Just try the read and handle ENOENT; checking first races with other processes and costs an extra system call.

concepts.name: Paths, URLs and the os module
concepts.summary: Build file paths portably with node:path, convert file URLs, and query the machine with node:os.
concepts.why: String-concatenated paths break on Windows and when scripts run from another folder.
concepts.body:
Never glue paths with `+ "/" +`. The `node:path` module knows the platform's separator and normalises `..` and duplicate slashes:

- `path.join("a", "b", "../c.txt")` → `a/c.txt` — joins and normalises segments.
- `path.resolve("data", "x.json")` → an **absolute** path, resolved against the current working directory unless a segment is already absolute.
- `path.dirname`, `path.basename(p, ".js")`, `path.extname` — take paths apart; `path.parse` returns all parts as an object.
- `path.relative(from, to)` — the path from one location to another.
- `path.sep` is `/` on POSIX and `\` on Windows; `path.posix` and `path.win32` force a style (use `posix` for URL-like paths).

The crucial distinction is **where relative paths resolve**: against `process.cwd()`, the directory the user launched Node from. To find a file next to your module regardless of where the process started, anchor on the module itself: `path.join(import.meta.dirname, "templates", "email.html")`.

ES modules identify themselves with a **file URL** (`import.meta.url`, e.g. `file:///home/me/app/main.js`). Most `fs` functions accept a `URL` directly, and `node:url` converts both ways with `fileURLToPath` and `pathToFileURL`. `new URL("./data.json", import.meta.url)` is a neat way to locate a sibling file.

The `node:os` module answers questions about the machine: `os.cpus().length` (or better, `os.availableParallelism()`) for sizing worker pools, `os.tmpdir()`, `os.homedir()`, `os.EOL`, `os.totalmem()` / `os.freemem()`, `os.platform()`.
takeaways: Use `path.join`/`path.resolve`, never string concatenation
Relative paths resolve against `process.cwd()`, not the module's folder
Anchor on `import.meta.dirname` or `new URL(..., import.meta.url)`
pitfalls: Using `path.join` to build URLs on Windows — it inserts backslashes; use `path.posix` or `URL`.

quiz.q: A script in /app/tools/gen.js reads path.resolve("tpl.txt"). The user runs `node tools/gen.js` from /app. Which file is read?
options: It throws because the path is relative
quiz.explain: path.resolve uses the current working directory (/app), not the script's folder.

concepts.name: The process object and exit codes
concepts.summary: Use the global process object for arguments, stdio, the working directory, exit codes and signals.
concepts.why: Correct exit codes and signal handling are how your program cooperates with shells, CI and container platforms.
concepts.body:
`process` is a global object describing the running Node process. The parts you will use:

- `process.argv` — command-line arguments; `[0]` is the node binary, `[1]` the script, the rest are yours.
- `process.env` — environment variables (next lesson).
- `process.cwd()` — current working directory; `process.chdir()` changes it.
- `process.stdout`, `process.stderr`, `process.stdin` — the standard streams. `console.log` writes to stdout, `console.error` to stderr. Send diagnostics to stderr so stdout stays clean for piping.
- `process.pid`, `process.platform`, `process.version`, `process.memoryUsage()`, `process.uptime()`.

**Exit codes** tell the caller whether you succeeded: 0 means success, anything else failure. Node exits with 0 when the event loop empties, and with 1 on an uncaught exception or unhandled rejection. To report failure yourself, prefer setting `process.exitCode = 1` and letting the program finish naturally. `process.exit(code)` stops *immediately*: pending writes to stdout, open file handles and in-flight requests are cut off, which can truncate output when piped.

**Signals** let other programs ask you to stop. Ctrl+C sends `SIGINT`; Docker, Kubernetes and systemd send `SIGTERM`. Without handlers Node exits right away. Listen with `process.on("SIGTERM", ...)` to finish work and close servers first — the basis of graceful shutdown.

The `"exit"` event fires as the process ends, but only synchronous code runs inside it. For async cleanup, use `"beforeExit"` (fires when the loop empties naturally) or handle the signal.
takeaways: `process.argv.slice(2)` are your arguments
Prefer `process.exitCode = n` over `process.exit(n)`
Results to stdout, diagnostics to stderr
Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM to shut down cleanly
pitfalls: Calling `process.exit()` right after writing output, truncating it when piped.

quiz.q: Why is process.exitCode = 1 usually better than process.exit(1)?
options: exitCode lets pending I/O finish before the process ends
exitCode also sends SIGTERM to child processes
quiz.explain: process.exit() terminates immediately, potentially dropping buffered output; exitCode just sets the code used at a natural exit.

concepts.name: Environment variables and .env files
concepts.summary: Read configuration from process.env, load .env files with --env-file, and validate config at startup.
concepts.why: Twelve-factor apps take secrets and settings from the environment, so the same code runs in dev, CI and production.
concepts.body:
Configuration that differs between environments — database URLs, API keys, ports, feature flags — belongs in **environment variables**, not in code. Node exposes them as `process.env`, a plain object whose values are **always strings** (or `undefined` if unset).

```bash
PORT=8080 LOG_LEVEL=debug node server.js
```

For local development you usually keep them in a `.env` file. Node 22 reads it natively, no `dotenv` package required:

- `node --env-file=.env server.js` — fails if the file is missing; `--env-file-if-exists` doesn't.
- Pass the flag several times; later files override earlier ones.
- Variables already set in the real environment win over the file, so production settings can't be overridden by a stray `.env`.
- From code: `process.loadEnvFile(".env")`, or `util.parseEnv(text)` to parse without touching `process.env`.

Commit a `.env.example` listing every variable with dummy values, and add `.env` to `.gitignore`.

Read and validate configuration **once, at startup**, in one module. Convert types explicitly — `Number(process.env.PORT)`, `process.env.DEBUG === "true"` — because `"false"` is a truthy string. Fail fast with a clear message if something required is missing; a crash at boot is much better than a `undefined` connection string discovered at 3 a.m.

`NODE_ENV=production` is a convention many libraries (Express included) check to disable debug features and enable caching. Set it in production, but don't use it as your only switch for app behaviour — explicit variables are clearer.
takeaways: `process.env` values are strings or undefined — convert explicitly
`node --env-file=.env` replaces the dotenv package
Validate all config once at startup and fail fast
pitfalls: Committing `.env` with real secrets to git.
Writing `if (process.env.FEATURE)` and enabling the feature when it is set to "false".

quiz.q: process.env.ENABLE_CACHE is set to the string "false". What does `if (process.env.ENABLE_CACHE)` do?
options: Runs the block, because a non-empty string is truthy
quiz.explain: Environment values are strings; "false" is a non-empty string and therefore truthy.

concepts.name: Command-line arguments and user input
concepts.summary: Parse flags with util.parseArgs, read lines interactively with readline/promises, and accept piped stdin.
concepts.why: Small CLI tools are one of the most common things people write in Node.
concepts.body:
`process.argv` gives raw strings. For real flags use the built-in **`util.parseArgs`**, which handles `--name value`, `--name=value`, short aliases and booleans:

- Declare `options` with a `type` (`"string"` or `"boolean"`), optional `short`, `default` and `multiple`.
- Set `allowPositionals: true` to accept bare arguments.
- Unknown flags throw by default (`strict: true`), so typos don't pass silently.

For interactive questions, use **`node:readline/promises`**. Create an interface over stdin/stdout, `await rl.question("Name? ")`, and `rl.close()` when done — an open interface keeps the process alive.

Tools that work well in pipelines also read **stdin**: `cat data.txt | node count.js`. `process.stdin` is a readable stream, so you can iterate it with `for await`, or use `readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin })` and `for await (const line of rl)` to get one line at a time. `process.stdin.isTTY` tells you whether a human is typing or data is piped in.

For output, keep it simple: `console.log` for results, `console.error` for messages. `util.styleText("red", "error")` adds colour without a dependency and is ignored automatically when output isn't a terminal in recent Node versions; `console.table` prints arrays of objects nicely.

When a CLI grows subcommands, help text and completion, a library like `commander` is reasonable, but many tools never need more than `parseArgs`.
takeaways: `util.parseArgs` handles flags, aliases and positionals without dependencies
`readline/promises` for questions; close the interface when finished
`for await` over a readline interface reads piped stdin line by line
pitfalls: Forgetting `rl.close()`, so the process hangs waiting for input.

quiz.q: With parseArgs in its default strict mode, what happens when the user passes an undeclared --verbose flag?
options: It is stored in values.verbose as true
quiz.explain: strict mode (the default) rejects unknown options so typos are caught.

concepts.name: Async patterns in Node
concepts.summary: From error-first callbacks to promises: promisify old APIs, run work concurrently, add timeouts and cancel with AbortSignal.
concepts.why: Real services juggle many I/O operations; doing them in the right order, in parallel, and cancellably is the job.
concepts.body:
Node's original convention is the **error-first callback**: the last argument is a function called as `cb(err, result)`. You will still meet it in older libraries. Every built-in now has a promise form (`node:fs/promises`, `node:timers/promises`, `node:dns/promises`, `node:stream/promises`), and `util.promisify(fn)` converts any error-first function into one that returns a promise.

With promises, the main skill is choosing **sequential vs concurrent**:

- `await a(); await b();` — b starts only after a finishes. Right when b needs a's result.
- `await Promise.all([a(), b()])` — both run at once; fails fast on the first rejection.
- `Promise.allSettled` when you want every outcome, even failures.

Unbounded concurrency is its own bug: `Promise.all(10_000 urls.map(fetch))` opens ten thousand sockets. Process big lists in batches or with a small pool.

**Cancellation** in Node uses the web-standard `AbortController`. Pass `signal` to `fetch`, `fs.readFile`, `setTimeout` from `timers/promises`, `events.once`, child processes and streams; calling `controller.abort()` makes them reject with an `AbortError`. For deadlines, `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` creates a signal that aborts by itself, and `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` combines signals.

`node:timers/promises` gives awaitable timers: `await setTimeout(500)` sleeps, and `for await (const _ of setInterval(1000))` ticks.

Finally, never leave a promise floating. A rejected promise nobody awaits becomes an **unhandled rejection**, which crashes Node by default. If you intentionally fire and forget, attach a `.catch()`.
takeaways: `util.promisify` converts error-first callback APIs
Independent work: `Promise.all`; dependent work: sequential `await`
Bound concurrency for big lists
Cancel with AbortController; deadlines with `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`
pitfalls: Awaiting inside a for loop for independent requests, making them needlessly sequential.
Firing a promise without await or .catch, causing an unhandled rejection crash.

quiz.q: You must call getUser(id) and getOrders(id); neither needs the other's result. What's best?
quiz.explain: Promise.all starts both at once and waits for both, halving the wall-clock time.

quiz.q: How do you give a fetch call a 2-second deadline in Node 22?
quiz.explain: fetch has no timeout option; an AbortSignal that aborts itself after 2000 ms is the standard way.

concepts.name: Events and EventEmitter
concepts.summary: Emit and listen to named events with EventEmitter, the pattern behind streams, servers and sockets.
concepts.why: Half of Node's core API is built on EventEmitter, so you need it to understand servers, streams and processes.
concepts.body:
An **EventEmitter** is an object that lets other code subscribe to named events. Node's servers, sockets, streams, child processes and `process` itself all extend it.

The core API:

- `emitter.on(name, listener)` — call `listener` every time `name` is emitted; `once` only for the next one.
- `emitter.emit(name, ...args)` — call every listener for `name`, in registration order, passing the args.
- `emitter.off(name, listener)` — remove a listener (you need the same function reference).

Two facts matter more than the API. First, **`emit` is synchronous**: all listeners run before `emit` returns, on the same call stack. A slow listener slows the emitter; a throwing listener throws out of `emit`. If you need async behaviour, the listener must schedule it.

Second, the event named **`"error"` is special**. If an emitter emits `"error"` and nobody listens, Node throws the error and — unless caught — crashes the process. Always attach an `error` listener to sockets, streams and anything else that can fail.

Bridging to async/await:

- `await once(emitter, "ready")` (from `node:events`) waits for a single event and rejects if `"error"` fires first.
- `for await (const [msg] of on(emitter, "message"))` turns events into an async iterator.

To write your own, extend `EventEmitter` in a class and call `this.emit(...)`. Node prints a **MaxListenersExceededWarning** when more than 10 listeners attach to one event — usually a leak where you add a listener per request and never remove it. Raise the limit with `setMaxListeners` only if it is genuinely intended.

Browsers' `EventTarget` also exists in Node; use it when you want web-compatible code, but most Node APIs speak EventEmitter.
takeaways: `emit` calls listeners synchronously, in order
An unhandled `'error'` event throws and usually crashes the process
`events.once` / `events.on` bridge events to async/await
pitfalls: Adding listeners inside a request handler and never removing them (memory leak + MaxListeners warning).

quiz.q: An emitter emits 'error' with no 'error' listener attached. What happens?
options: The error is thrown, typically crashing the process
Node logs a warning and continues
The error is queued until a listener is added
quiz.explain: 'error' is special: without a listener, emit throws the error.

concepts.name: Streams: reading and writing in chunks
concepts.summary: Process data piece by piece with readable, writable and transform streams, and connect them safely with pipeline().
concepts.why: Streams let you handle files and network data far larger than memory with constant memory use.
concepts.body:
A **stream** delivers data in chunks over time instead of all at once. Four kinds exist:

- **Readable** — a source: `fs.createReadStream`, an HTTP request on the server, `process.stdin`.
- **Writable** — a destination: `fs.createWriteStream`, an HTTP response, `process.stdout`.
- **Duplex** — both, independently (a TCP socket).
- **Transform** — a duplex whose output is computed from its input (`zlib.createGzip()`, a CSV parser).

Copying a 5 GB log with `readFile` + `writeFile` needs 5 GB of RAM; with streams it needs about 64 KB at a time.

The right way to connect streams is **`pipeline`** from `node:stream/promises`:

```javascript
await pipeline(createReadStream("in.log"), createGzip(), createWriteStream("in.log.gz"));
```

It wires each stream to the next, propagates errors from any stage, destroys all streams on failure, and resolves when everything finishes. The older `a.pipe(b)` does none of the error handling — a failing source leaves the destination open and leaks file descriptors.

Readable streams are **async iterables**, so the simplest way to consume one is `for await (const chunk of stream)`. Chunks are `Buffer`s unless you set an encoding (`createReadStream(path, { encoding: "utf8" })`) or the stream is in **object mode**.

To write your own transform, `new Transform({ transform(chunk, enc, cb) { cb(null, result) } })` works, but you can also pass an **async generator function** as a pipeline stage — it receives the previous stage as an iterable and yields output. That is often the most readable option.

Node also implements web streams (`ReadableStream`, used by `fetch` bodies); `Readable.fromWeb` and `Readable.toWeb` convert between the two.
takeaways: Streams move data in chunks with bounded memory
Connect stages with `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises`, not `.pipe()`
Readables are async iterables; async generators make easy transforms
pitfalls: Using `.pipe()` without error handling, leaking open files when a stage fails.
Assuming a chunk boundary aligns with a line or record boundary.

quiz.q: What does stream.pipeline do that a.pipe(b).pipe(c) does not?
options: Makes the copy faster by using threads
Reads the whole input into memory first
Forwards errors from any stage and destroys all streams on failure
quiz.explain: pipeline handles errors and cleanup across all stages; .pipe() leaves that to you.

concepts.name: Building an HTTP server with node:http
concepts.summary: Create a web server with node:http: route requests, read bodies, set status and headers, and send responses.
concepts.why: Every Node web framework, Express included, is a layer over this module; knowing it makes frameworks unmysterious.
concepts.body:
`http.createServer(handler)` returns a server that calls `handler(req, res)` for each request. `server.listen(port)` starts accepting connections.

- `req` is an **IncomingMessage** (a readable stream): `req.method`, `req.url` (path plus query string, e.g. `/users?page=2`), and `req.headers` with **lower-cased** names.
- `res` is a **ServerResponse** (a writable stream): set `res.statusCode` or call `res.writeHead(status, headers)`, `res.setHeader(name, value)`, write with `res.write(chunk)`, and always finish with `res.end(body)`.

Parse the URL with the WHATWG `URL` class: `new URL(req.url, "http://localhost")` gives you `pathname` and `searchParams`.

The request **body** is not parsed for you — it arrives as a stream. Collect it with `for await (const chunk of req)`, concatenate the Buffers, then `JSON.parse`. Cap the size so a client can't send you a gigabyte, and respond 400 on invalid JSON.

Things the raw module leaves to you, which frameworks provide: routing, body parsing, content-type negotiation, cookies, error handling. Note also:

- Every code path must end the response, or the client hangs until it times out.
- A thrown error inside an `async` handler is an unhandled rejection — wrap the handler in try/catch and answer 500.
- Headers must be set before the first `write`; afterwards `res.headersSent` is true and setting them throws.

The `node:https` module works the same with TLS certificates, and `node:http2` supports HTTP/2. In production you'll often run plain HTTP behind a load balancer that terminates TLS.
takeaways: `req` is a readable stream, `res` a writable stream
You must parse URLs and bodies yourself, and always `res.end()`
Header names in `req.headers` are lower-case
Catch errors in async handlers and answer with a status code
pitfalls: Forgetting to end the response on one code path, leaving the client hanging.
Reading request bodies without a size limit.

quiz.q: A client sends JSON in a POST. Where is it in a plain node:http handler?
options: In the req stream; you must read and parse it
quiz.explain: node:http doesn't parse bodies; req is a readable stream you consume (frameworks add req.body).

concepts.name: Making HTTP requests with fetch
concepts.summary: Call APIs with the built-in fetch: check status, send JSON, set timeouts, stream responses, and reuse connections.
concepts.why: Talking to other services is part of nearly every backend, and fetch is now the standard way.
concepts.body:
Node 22 has a global, web-compatible **`fetch`**, implemented by the **undici** HTTP client. No `axios` or `node-fetch` needed.

The most important rule: **fetch only rejects on network failures**, not on HTTP errors. A 404 or 500 resolves normally with `res.ok === false`. Always check `res.ok` (or `res.status`) before using the body.

Sending JSON means doing it yourself:

```javascript
await fetch(url, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify(data),
});
```

Reading the body: `await res.json()`, `res.text()`, `res.arrayBuffer()`, or `res.body`, a web `ReadableStream` you can iterate with `for await` or convert with `Readable.fromWeb` for piping to a file. A body can be read only once. If you don't need it, call `await res.body?.cancel()` so the connection can be reused.

There is **no default timeout** you control per request; pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`. An aborted request rejects with an error named `TimeoutError` (from `timeout`) or `AbortError`.

Behind the scenes undici keeps a **connection pool** per origin with keep-alive, so repeated calls to the same API are cheap. For advanced tuning (pool size, proxies, custom TLS), install the `undici` package and pass a `dispatcher`.

Retries are your job: retry idempotent requests (GET, PUT, DELETE) on network errors and 502/503/504 with exponential backoff and a cap, and respect `Retry-After` on 429.

`FormData`, `Blob`, `Headers`, `Request` and `Response` are globals too, so multipart uploads and mocking responses work like in the browser.
takeaways: fetch resolves on HTTP errors — check `res.ok`
Use `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` for deadlines
Bodies are streams, readable once; cancel unused ones
pitfalls: Calling `res.json()` on an error response and getting a confusing parse error instead of the status.

quiz.q: fetch() to an endpoint returns HTTP 503. What happens?
options: The promise resolves; res.ok is false and res.status is 503
The promise rejects with a TypeError
Node emits an 'error' event on process
quiz.explain: fetch only rejects for network-level failures; HTTP error statuses resolve normally.

concepts.name: Error handling in Node applications
concepts.summary: Distinguish operational from programmer errors, use error codes and causes, and handle uncaught exceptions and rejections.
concepts.why: How a service fails decides whether an incident is a logged warning or a crashed, corrupted process.
concepts.body:
Two categories of error need different treatment:

- **Operational errors** are expected failures of a correct program: file not found, connection refused, invalid user input, a timeout. Handle them — retry, return a 4xx, fall back to defaults.
- **Programmer errors** are bugs: `undefined is not a function`, a wrong argument type. You can't meaningfully recover; log, crash, and let a supervisor restart the process.

Node's errors carry a stable **`code`** property (`ENOENT`, `ECONNREFUSED`, `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE`). Branch on `err.code`, never on message text, which can change between versions. Do the same in your own code: subclass `Error`, set `name` and a `code`, and add context fields.

When you catch and rethrow, keep the original with **`cause`**: `throw new Error("loading user 42 failed", { cause: err })`. Logs and `util.inspect` then show both stacks.

Async rules:

- `try/catch` only catches a rejection if you `await` the promise inside the `try`.
- A promise rejection nobody handles triggers `unhandledRejection`; since Node 15 the default is to **crash** with exit code 1.
- A throw that escapes everything triggers `uncaughtException` and also crashes.

You can listen for both on `process`, but use them only to **log and exit** (`process.exit(1)` after flushing logs). After an uncaught exception, the process may be in an inconsistent state — half-written data, held locks — so continuing is dangerous. Run under something that restarts you (systemd, Docker restart policy, Kubernetes).

Finally, throw `Error` objects, not strings: only errors have stack traces.
takeaways: Handle operational errors; crash and restart on programmer errors
Branch on `err.code`, wrap with `{ cause }` to keep context
Unhandled rejections crash Node by default
Use uncaught handlers only to log and exit
pitfalls: Catching `uncaughtException` and continuing to serve requests from a corrupted state.
`try { promise } catch` without `await`, so the rejection escapes.

quiz.q: Which error should a service typically handle and keep running?
options: TypeError: user.name is not a function
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
An ECONNREFUSED when calling a downstream API
quiz.explain: A refused connection is an operational error you can retry or report; the others are bugs.

quiz.q: Why is checking err.code better than matching err.message?
options: Codes are stable API; messages may change between versions
Messages are not available on system errors
err.message is undefined for async errors
quiz.explain: Node documents error codes as stable, while message text is not guaranteed.

concepts.name: Debugging Node with the inspector
concepts.summary: Debug with --inspect and Chrome DevTools or VS Code: breakpoints, stepping, watching variables, and debugging tests.
concepts.why: A real debugger finds bugs faster than scattering console.log calls.
concepts.body:
Node includes the V8 **inspector**, the same debugging protocol Chrome uses. Start your program with a flag:

- `node --inspect app.js` — runs normally and listens for a debugger on `127.0.0.1:9229`.
- `node --inspect-brk app.js` — pauses before the first line, so you can set breakpoints in startup code.
- `node --inspect-wait app.js` — waits for a debugger to attach, then runs.

Then attach a client:

- **Chrome**: open `chrome://inspect`, click "Open dedicated DevTools for Node". You get Sources, breakpoints, the console in your program's context, plus Memory and Performance tabs.
- **VS Code**: the JavaScript Debug Terminal auto-attaches to any `node` you start in it, or create a launch configuration. Breakpoints are set in the editor gutter.

Inside the debugger you can step over/into/out, inspect the call stack (including async frames, so you see which `await` led here), add watch expressions, and set **conditional breakpoints** or **logpoints** that print without pausing. A `debugger;` statement in code acts as a breakpoint when a debugger is attached.

Never expose the inspector on a public interface: `--inspect=0.0.0.0` gives anyone who can reach the port full code execution in your process. To debug a remote machine, keep the default localhost binding and use an SSH tunnel.

Other helpful tools: `node inspect app.js` is a terminal debugger; `NODE_DEBUG=http,net` turns on internal debug logs of core modules; `console.trace()` prints the current stack; `--enable-source-maps` makes stack traces point to TypeScript sources. For tests, `node --inspect-brk --test` lets you step through a failing test.
concepts.code:
# Pause at the first line and attach Chrome DevTools (chrome://inspect)
node --inspect-brk server.js

# Debug a single failing test file
node --inspect-brk --test test/user.test.js

# Readable stack traces for transpiled code
node --enable-source-maps dist/server.js

# Internal debug logging from core modules
NODE_DEBUG=http,net node server.js

# Remote host: keep the inspector on localhost and tunnel it
ssh -L 9229:127.0.0.1:9229 user@server   # then attach to localhost:9229
takeaways: `--inspect` / `--inspect-brk` enable the debugger on port 9229
Attach via chrome://inspect or VS Code's JavaScript Debug Terminal
Conditional breakpoints and logpoints avoid edit-restart cycles
Never bind the inspector to a public interface
pitfalls: Running `--inspect=0.0.0.0` on a server, which allows remote code execution.

quiz.q: You need to break inside code that runs during module loading. Which flag fits?
quiz.explain: --inspect-brk pauses before user code starts, giving you time to set breakpoints.

concepts.name: Testing with node:test
concepts.summary: Write and run tests with Node's built-in test runner and assert module, including mocks, async tests and coverage.
concepts.why: Built-in testing means zero-dependency, fast tests that work in every Node project.
concepts.body:
Node ships a complete test runner in **`node:test`** — no Jest or Mocha required for most projects.

- Organise with `describe(name, fn)` and `it(name, fn)` (or `test`). Async functions just work: the test waits for the promise.
- Hooks: `before`, `after`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach`.
- Modifiers: `it.skip`, `it.todo`, `it.only` (run with `--test-only`).

Assertions come from **`node:assert/strict`**: `equal` (strict `===`), `deepEqual` (structural), `ok`, `match` (regex), `throws` for sync code and **`await assert.rejects(promise, matcher)`** for async code. Always use the `strict` variant; the legacy one uses loose `==`.

Run tests with `node --test`. With no arguments it finds files matching patterns such as `**/*.test.js`, `**/*-test.js` and files in `test/` directories, and runs each **file in its own process** in parallel. Useful flags:

- `--watch` reruns on change.
- `--test-name-pattern="login"` filters tests.
- `--experimental-test-coverage` prints line/branch coverage.
- `--test-reporter=spec|dot|tap|junit` changes output (junit for CI).

**Mocking** is built in through the `t.mock` / `mock` object: `mock.fn()` creates a spy recording calls, `mock.method(obj, "name", impl)` replaces a method and restores it after the test, and `mock.timers.enable()` fakes `setTimeout` and `Date` so time-dependent code runs instantly.

Good tests target behaviour: call the public function or the HTTP endpoint, assert on outputs and side effects. Keep each test independent — create fresh state in `beforeEach` rather than relying on test order.
takeaways: `node --test` runs `*.test.js` files, each in its own process
Use `node:assert/strict`; `assert.rejects` for async errors
`mock.fn`, `mock.method` and `mock.timers` cover most mocking
pitfalls: Writing `assert.rejects(promise)` without `await`, so the test passes before the check runs.

quiz.q: Which assertion correctly checks that an async function rejects?
quiz.explain: assert.rejects awaits the promise and checks that it rejects; throws only sees synchronous throws.

concepts.name: Offloading CPU work to worker threads
concepts.summary: Run CPU-heavy JavaScript on worker_threads so the main event loop stays responsive, passing data by message.
concepts.why: A single slow computation in the main thread freezes every request your server is handling.
concepts.body:
Node runs your JavaScript on one thread. That's perfect for I/O, but a CPU-bound task — hashing, image resizing, parsing a huge JSON file, a tight numeric loop — blocks the event loop: no other requests are served, no timers fire, until it finishes.

**`node:worker_threads`** runs JavaScript on additional threads. Each **Worker** has its own V8 isolate, event loop and module graph; workers don't share variables with the main thread. They communicate by **messages**:

- Create one with `new Worker(new URL("./worker.js", import.meta.url), { workerData })`.
- In the worker, `workerData` holds the initial input, and `parentPort.postMessage(result)` sends results back.
- The parent listens for `"message"`, `"error"` (an uncaught exception in the worker) and `"exit"`.

Messages are copied with the **structured clone** algorithm — plain objects, arrays, Maps, Dates, typed arrays work; functions and class instances' prototypes don't survive. Large binary data can be **transferred** instead of copied by listing an `ArrayBuffer` in the transfer list.

Starting a worker costs a few milliseconds and some megabytes, so don't spawn one per request. For anything frequent, keep a **pool** of long-lived workers sized to the CPU count (`os.availableParallelism()`); libraries like `piscina` do this well.

Workers are the wrong tool for I/O: the main thread already does I/O concurrently. Use them only when profiling shows JavaScript computation is the bottleneck. Native operations such as `crypto.pbkdf2`, `zlib` and `fs` already run on libuv's thread pool when you use their async versions — prefer those over hand-rolled workers.
takeaways: CPU-bound JS blocks the event loop; workers run it on other threads
Workers share nothing by default and talk via structured-clone messages
Reuse workers through a pool; never spawn one per request
pitfalls: Using worker threads for I/O-bound work, adding overhead with no benefit.

quiz.q: Which task benefits most from a worker thread?
options: Resizing a large image in pure JavaScript
Reading a config file at startup
quiz.explain: Pure-JS image processing is CPU-bound; the others are I/O that Node already does concurrently.

concepts.name: Backpressure and custom streams
concepts.summary: Understand highWaterMark, write() returning false and 'drain', and build Transform streams that respect backpressure.
concepts.why: Ignoring backpressure is how a fast producer and slow consumer turn into an out-of-memory crash.
concepts.body:
Every stream has an internal buffer whose target size is the **highWaterMark** (64 KiB for byte streams in Node 22, 16 objects in object mode). It is a threshold, not a hard limit, and it is how **backpressure** works: the mechanism by which a slow consumer tells a fast producer to wait.

On the writable side, `writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean. `false` means "my buffer is above the highWaterMark — stop until I emit `'drain'`". The data is still accepted; nothing enforces the pause. Code that ignores the return value keeps buffering, and memory grows until the process dies.

```javascript
if (!out.write(chunk)) await once(out, "drain");
```

On the readable side, a stream reads ahead only until its buffer reaches the highWaterMark, then waits for the consumer. In a custom `Readable`, `push()` returning `false` is your signal to stop producing until `_read()` is called again.

The good news: **`pipeline()` and `for await` handle all of this for you.** `pipeline` pauses sources when destinations fill up; async iteration only pulls the next chunk when your loop body finishes. Manual `on("data")` handlers are where backpressure gets lost, because `'data'` keeps firing however slowly you process it.

When writing a `Transform`, call the callback only when you have finished with the chunk, push output with `this.push()`, and use `flush(callback)` to emit anything buffered at the end. Errors go to `callback(err)`, which destroys the stream and propagates through `pipeline`.

Tune `highWaterMark` deliberately: bigger buffers improve throughput for large sequential copies, smaller ones reduce memory per connection. Measure before changing it.
takeaways: `write()` returning false means wait for `'drain'`
`pipeline` and `for await` apply backpressure automatically
In Transforms, call the callback when done and use `flush` for trailing output
pitfalls: Writing in a loop and ignoring `write()`'s return value, buffering unbounded data.
Consuming with `on('data')` and slow async work, which defeats backpressure.

quiz.q: writable.write(chunk) returns false. What does that mean?
options: The chunk was rejected and must be resent
The buffer is above highWaterMark; pause until 'drain'
An error occurred and 'error' will follow
quiz.explain: The chunk was buffered, but the producer should stop writing until 'drain' fires.

concepts.name: The event loop phases and libuv
concepts.summary: Learn the event loop's phases, where nextTick, promises, setImmediate and timers run, and what libuv's thread pool does.
concepts.why: Explains surprising callback orders, starved I/O, and why some 'async' operations are slower than others.
concepts.body:
Node's event loop, provided by **libuv**, cycles through **phases**, each with a queue of callbacks:

- **timers** — expired `setTimeout` / `setInterval` callbacks.
- **pending callbacks** — some deferred system errors.
- **poll** — waits for new I/O events and runs their callbacks (socket data, completed file reads). If nothing else is scheduled, the loop blocks here.
- **check** — `setImmediate` callbacks.
- **close callbacks** — `'close'` events of handles such as sockets.

Between every individual callback, Node drains two higher-priority queues: first the **`process.nextTick`** queue, then the **promise microtask** queue (`then` callbacks, code after `await`). That is why a promise continuation always runs before the next timer, and why recursive `nextTick` (or an endless chain of resolved promises) can **starve** I/O completely.

Practical consequences:

- Inside an I/O callback, `setImmediate` always runs before `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, because check comes right after poll. From the main module their order is not guaranteed.
- `setTimeout(fn, 10)` means "not before 10 ms", never "exactly at 10 ms".
- Prefer `queueMicrotask` or `setImmediate` over `process.nextTick` unless you specifically need to run before any other async work.

Network I/O uses the OS's non-blocking mechanisms (epoll, kqueue, IOCP) directly. But file system calls, `dns.lookup`, and CPU-heavy `crypto`/`zlib` work run on libuv's **thread pool**, which has only **4 threads** by default (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, max 1024, set before startup). Many concurrent `fs` or `pbkdf2` calls queue behind each other there — a frequent hidden bottleneck.

Measure loop health with `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()`; consistently high delay means something is blocking.
takeaways: Phases: timers → pending → poll → check → close
nextTick then promise microtasks run between every callback
fs, dns.lookup, crypto and zlib use libuv's 4-thread pool by default
Starving the loop with microtasks blocks I/O
pitfalls: Using `process.nextTick` recursively and starving I/O.
Running hundreds of concurrent fs or crypto calls and blaming the disk for thread-pool queuing.

quiz.q: Inside an fs.readFile callback, you schedule setTimeout(a, 0) and setImmediate(b). Which runs first?
quiz.explain: After the poll phase the loop moves to check (setImmediate) before wrapping round to timers.

quiz.q: Your server makes many parallel crypto.pbkdf2 calls and latency climbs. Which setting is most relevant?
quiz.explain: Async pbkdf2 runs on libuv's thread pool, which defaults to 4 threads.

concepts.name: Worker pools, shared memory and cluster
concepts.summary: Scale across cores: pool worker threads, share memory with SharedArrayBuffer, and fork HTTP servers with cluster.
concepts.why: One Node process uses one core for JavaScript; production servers usually need all of them.
concepts.body:
There are two ways to use more than one CPU core from Node, and they solve different problems.

**Worker thread pools** speed up CPU-heavy *tasks* inside one process. Create N long-lived workers (N ≈ `os.availableParallelism()` minus one for the main thread), queue tasks, and hand each to an idle worker. A pool must handle a worker crashing (replace it, reject its task) and support shutdown. `piscina` is the standard library for this.

To avoid copying large data:

- **Transfer** an `ArrayBuffer` (`postMessage(buf, [buf])`) — ownership moves, the sender's copy becomes unusable, zero copying.
- **Share** a `SharedArrayBuffer`: both threads see the same memory. Coordinate with `Atomics` (`Atomics.add`, `Atomics.wait`/`notify`) because plain reads and writes race.
- A `MessageChannel` gives two workers a direct port to talk without the main thread.

**Cluster** scales *request handling*. `node:cluster` forks the whole program into several processes; the primary process distributes incoming connections to workers (round-robin by default, except on Windows), and all of them appear to listen on the same port. Each worker is a full Node process with its own memory, so in-memory state — sessions, caches, rate-limit counters — is **not shared**. Move it to Redis or a database.

In containerised deployments, you'll often skip cluster entirely: run one Node process per container and let Kubernetes or the load balancer scale replicas. That gives simpler processes, better isolation and per-instance health checks. Cluster still fits single-VM deployments; PM2's cluster mode wraps the same module.

Whatever you choose, make the processes **stateless** so any instance can serve any request.
takeaways: Worker pools parallelise CPU tasks; cluster parallelises request handling
Transfer or share buffers to avoid copying large data; guard shared memory with Atomics
Cluster workers share nothing — keep state in external stores
pitfalls: Keeping sessions or rate limits in process memory, then adding cluster and getting inconsistent behaviour.

quiz.q: After switching an app to cluster with 8 workers, logged-in users are randomly logged out. Likely cause?
options: Sessions were stored in process memory, which each worker has separately
quiz.explain: Each worker is a separate process; an in-memory session store exists only in the worker that created it.

concepts.name: Running other programs: child_process
concepts.summary: Run external commands with execFile, spawn and fork; stream their output, pass input, and avoid shell injection.
concepts.why: Build tools, CLIs and backends constantly shell out to git, ffmpeg, image tools or other Node scripts.
concepts.body:
`node:child_process` starts other programs. Pick the function by what you need:

- **`execFile(file, args)`** — run a program and buffer its output; great for short commands like `git rev-parse HEAD`. Output beyond `maxBuffer` (1 MB) is an error.
- **`spawn(cmd, args)`** — returns a `ChildProcess` with `stdout`/`stderr`/`stdin` **streams**; use it for long-running or chatty processes and large output. `stdio: "inherit"` connects the child directly to your terminal.
- **`exec(commandString)`** — runs a string through a shell (`/bin/sh` or `cmd.exe`). Convenient for pipes and globs, dangerous with user input.
- **`fork(modulePath)`** — spawns a new Node process with an **IPC channel**, so parent and child exchange objects with `send()` / `on("message")`.

The security rule: **never build a shell command from untrusted input.** `exec(\`convert ${filename} out.png\`)` with a filename like `x; rm -rf ~` runs both commands. `execFile` and `spawn` without `shell: true` pass arguments directly to the program, so no shell parsing happens.

Exit status arrives on the `'close'` event (after stdio streams finish) as `code`, or `signal` if killed. A non-zero code is not an exception with `spawn` — check it yourself. The promisified `execFile` rejects on non-zero exit, with `stdout`/`stderr` attached to the error.

Control: `child.kill("SIGTERM")`, the `timeout` and `signal` (AbortSignal) options, `cwd` and `env` for the child's environment. The `*Sync` variants block the event loop; fine in build scripts, not in servers.

Each child is a full OS process — tens of milliseconds to start, separate memory. For heavy JavaScript work prefer worker threads; use child processes for other programs or isolation.
takeaways: `execFile` for short commands, `spawn` for streaming, `fork` for Node-to-Node IPC
Never interpolate user input into `exec` or `shell: true` commands
Check the exit code; handle the `'error'` event
pitfalls: Using `exec` with string interpolation of user-controlled values.
Buffering huge output with exec/execFile and hitting maxBuffer.

quiz.q: You need to run ffmpeg on a user-uploaded filename. Which call is safe?
quiz.explain: spawn without a shell passes the filename as a single argument, so shell metacharacters are inert.

concepts.name: Profiling CPU and event-loop performance
concepts.summary: Find bottlenecks with --cpu-prof, DevTools and flame graphs, measure with perf_hooks, and watch event-loop delay.
concepts.why: Performance work without measurement optimises the wrong thing; profiles show where time actually goes.
concepts.body:
Start every performance investigation with a reproducible **load** (`autocannon` for HTTP, a benchmark script for libraries) and a number to improve: latency percentiles, throughput, or event-loop delay.

**CPU profiling** shows which functions consume time:

- `node --cpu-prof app.js` writes a `.cpuprofile` file on exit; open it in Chrome DevTools (Performance tab) or VS Code. `--cpu-prof-dir` sets the location.
- Or attach DevTools via `--inspect` and record in the Performance/Profiler panel while load runs.
- Read it as a **flame graph**: wide bars are where time goes. Look for your own functions near the top of wide stacks — JSON serialisation, regexes, sync crypto, deep cloning, logging are frequent culprits.
- `node --prof` plus `node --prof-process` is the lower-level V8 tick profiler, useful on servers without a GUI.

**Event-loop delay** is the best single health metric for a Node service: how late callbacks run. `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()` gives a histogram (`p50`, `p99`, `max` in nanoseconds). A rising p99 means something synchronous is hogging the thread.

**Measuring code**: `performance.now()` for durations, `performance.mark`/`measure` for named spans, `performance.timerify(fn)` to time a function, and `PerformanceObserver` to collect entries, including GC events (`entryTypes: ["gc"]`).

Typical fixes, in order of payoff: do less work (cache, paginate), avoid sync APIs on hot paths, move CPU work to workers, then micro-optimise. Benchmark micro-optimisations properly — V8's JIT makes naive timing loops misleading — and re-profile after each change.
takeaways: Measure under realistic load before optimising
`--cpu-prof` + flame graphs show where CPU time goes
Event-loop delay (p99) is the key health metric
Fix algorithmic waste and sync work before micro-optimising
pitfalls: Optimising based on intuition or a micro-benchmark without profiling the real workload.

quiz.q: Your API's p99 latency spikes while CPU is moderate and the DB is fast. Which metric best confirms the event loop is being blocked?
quiz.explain: High event-loop delay means callbacks are running late because synchronous work occupies the thread.

concepts.name: Security essentials for Node apps
concepts.summary: Harden Node services: dependency hygiene, input validation, injection and path traversal, secrets, and the permission model.
concepts.why: Node apps run with your full privileges and pull in hundreds of packages; small mistakes become breaches.
concepts.body:
Most Node vulnerabilities come from a handful of patterns. Learn to spot them.

**Supply chain.** Your dependency tree is code you run. Commit the lockfile, install with `npm ci`, run `npm audit` in CI, keep dependencies current, and be wary of tiny new packages and typo-squatted names. `npm ci --ignore-scripts` blocks install-time scripts where your build allows it.

**Injection.** Never concatenate untrusted input into SQL (use parameterised queries), shell commands (`execFile` with an args array, not `exec`), `eval`/`new Function`, or regexes (catastrophic backtracking — **ReDoS** — can freeze the event loop).

**Path traversal.** A user-supplied filename like `../../etc/passwd` escapes your folder. Resolve the path and verify it stays inside the allowed root before reading.

**Prototype pollution.** Recursively merging untrusted JSON can set `__proto__` and change every object's behaviour. Validate input against a schema, use `Object.create(null)` or `Map` for dictionaries, and avoid hand-written deep merges.

**Denial of service.** Limit request body sizes, set timeouts (`server.requestTimeout`, `headersTimeout`), paginate queries, and keep CPU-heavy work off the main thread.

**Secrets.** Load from the environment or a secrets manager; never log them or commit them. Compare tokens with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.

**Least privilege.** Don't run as root. Node 22 includes a **permission model**: start with `--permission` and the process cannot touch the file system, spawn children or start workers unless you grant it, e.g. `--allow-fs-read=/app --allow-fs-write=/tmp`. Check at runtime with `process.permission.has("fs.write", path)`. It limits damage from compromised code, but it is not a sandbox for malicious code.

Keep Node itself patched: security releases land on LTS lines regularly.
takeaways: Lockfile + `npm ci` + `npm audit`; minimise dependencies
Parameterise queries and avoid shells to prevent injection
Resolve and check paths to stop traversal
`--permission` restricts fs, child processes and workers
pitfalls: Checking `userPath.includes('..')` instead of resolving and comparing the final path.
Treating the permission model as a sandbox for untrusted code.

quiz.q: A route serves files with readFile(path.join(root, req.query.name)). What's the main risk?
options: Path traversal to files outside root
quiz.explain: A name with ../ segments can resolve outside the root directory unless you resolve and check it.

quiz.q: What does starting Node with --permission do by default?
options: Denies file system access, child processes and workers unless explicitly allowed
Encrypts all files the process writes
Runs the process as an unprivileged OS user
quiz.explain: The permission model restricts fs, child_process and worker_threads until you grant access with --allow-* flags.

concepts.name: V8 memory, leaks and heap snapshots
concepts.summary: Understand V8's heap spaces and GC, size the heap for containers, and find memory leaks with heap snapshots.
concepts.why: Memory leaks are the classic slow-burn production incident in long-running Node services.
concepts.body:
V8 manages a garbage-collected **heap** per isolate. It is generational:

- **New space** (young generation) holds fresh objects. A fast *scavenger* copies survivors; most objects die here cheaply.
- **Old space** holds objects that survived a couple of scavenges. It is collected by **mark-sweep-compact**, mostly concurrent and incremental, but with some pauses.
- **Large object space**, code space, and others hold special cases.

`Buffer`s and `ArrayBuffer`s live *outside* the JS heap (counted in `process.memoryUsage().external` and `arrayBuffers`), so RSS can exceed heap size.

The old-space limit is set by `--max-old-space-size` (MB). The default depends on the Node version and the memory it detects, so set it explicitly in containers. Leave headroom for RSS beyond the heap: a common choice is about 75% of the container limit. When the heap can't grow, V8 crashes with "JavaScript heap out of memory".

A **leak** in JavaScript means something still *references* data you no longer need. Usual suspects: unbounded caches and Maps, listeners added per request, closures held by timers, global arrays used as queues, and per-request data stashed on long-lived objects.

To find one, compare **heap snapshots**:

- Take a snapshot, run load, take another (DevTools Memory tab via `--inspect`, `v8.writeHeapSnapshot()`, or `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2`).
- Use the Comparison view to see which constructors grew, then follow **retainers** to the root keeping them alive.
- Snapshots pause the process and need roughly 2x the heap in memory; avoid them on a struggling production instance without capacity.

Cheaper signals: `--trace-gc`, `v8.getHeapStatistics()`, and `--heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=N` to capture evidence automatically before an OOM. Use `WeakMap`, `WeakRef` and LRU caches with size limits to make retention explicit.
takeaways: Young generation is scavenged cheaply; old space uses mark-sweep-compact
Set `--max-old-space-size` below the container limit, leaving headroom
Leaks are unwanted references; compare heap snapshots and follow retainers
Buffers live outside the JS heap
pitfalls: Raising `--max-old-space-size` to hide a leak, which only delays the crash.
Taking heap snapshots on an instance with no spare memory and triggering the OOM yourself.

quiz.q: Heap usage climbs steadily under constant load and never drops after GC. What's the next diagnostic step?
options: Take two heap snapshots under load and compare them
quiz.explain: Comparing snapshots shows which objects accumulate and what retains them; raising the limit just postpones the crash.

concepts.name: Native addons and Node-API
concepts.summary: How C/C++ and Rust code plugs into Node through Node-API, how addons are built and shipped, and when to avoid them.
concepts.why: Many popular packages (database drivers, image libraries, bcrypt) are native addons; you need to debug, ship and occasionally write them.
concepts.body:
A **native addon** is a shared library (`.node` file) that Node loads like a module. It lets JavaScript call C, C++ or Rust code: to reuse an existing library (libvips, SQLite), to reach OS APIs Node doesn't expose, or occasionally for raw speed.

Modern addons use **Node-API** (N-API), a stable C ABI maintained by Node itself. Its key property is **ABI stability**: an addon compiled against Node-API version N runs on every later Node version without recompiling. Older addons that used V8 and NAN directly had to be rebuilt for every Node major. Wrappers make Node-API pleasant: `node-addon-api` for C++, `napi-rs` for Rust.

Building and shipping:

- `node-gyp` (with a `binding.gyp`) or `cmake-js` compile the addon; this needs Python and a C/C++ toolchain on the machine.
- Because users rarely have compilers, packages ship **prebuilt binaries** per platform/architecture — via `prebuildify`, or separate optional-dependency packages per platform (the approach napi-rs uses).
- In ESM, load a `.node` file with `createRequire(import.meta.url)` and `require()`.

Writing one, the rules that bite:

- JavaScript values are only valid within a **handle scope**; keep long-lived ones as **references**.
- Never block the main thread: long work belongs in an `AsyncWorker` running on the libuv thread pool.
- Calling back into JS from other threads requires a **thread-safe function**.
- An addon can be loaded by several worker threads at once, so keep global state per instance (`napi_set_instance_data`), not in C++ globals.

Before reaching for an addon, consider **WebAssembly**: portable, sandboxed, no compile step for users, and often fast enough. Many former native packages now ship WASM builds.
takeaways: Node-API gives a stable ABI: build once, run on later Node versions
Ship prebuilt binaries; users shouldn't need compilers
Do long work in AsyncWorker; use thread-safe functions for cross-thread callbacks
Consider WebAssembly before writing an addon
pitfalls: Doing heavy work synchronously inside an addon function, blocking the event loop.

quiz.q: Why did the move from NAN to Node-API matter so much for addon users?
options: Node-API addons run in a separate process
Node-API automatically converts C++ to JavaScript
Node-API is ABI-stable, so addons needn't be recompiled for each Node major
Node-API removes the need for a C compiler entirely
quiz.explain: ABI stability means one compiled binary keeps working across Node versions.

concepts.name: AsyncLocalStorage and async context
concepts.summary: Carry request-scoped context such as request IDs through async calls with AsyncLocalStorage, and know what async_hooks underlies it.
concepts.why: Logging, tracing and per-request state without threading a context argument through every function.
concepts.body:
In a server, many requests interleave on one thread, so a global "current request" variable is wrong as soon as you `await`. **`AsyncLocalStorage`** (from `node:async_hooks`) solves this: it gives each logical async flow its own store, which follows the code through `await`, promise callbacks, timers and event-emitter callbacks created inside that flow.

The API is small:

- `als.run(store, fn)` — run `fn` with `store` as the context; everything `fn` starts asynchronously sees the same store.
- `als.getStore()` — read the current store anywhere below, or `undefined` outside any `run`.
- `als.enterWith(store)` — set the store for the rest of the current synchronous execution; avoid it except in special integrations.

The classic use is a **request ID** or trace context: middleware calls `als.run({ requestId }, next)` and your logger reads `als.getStore()?.requestId`, so every log line is correlated without passing anything around. OpenTelemetry and APM agents use the same mechanism.

Pitfalls come from context that is captured at the wrong time. Callback-based libraries that keep their own queue of callbacks (some connection pools) may run your callback in another request's context. `AsyncResource.bind(fn)` or `AsyncLocalStorage.bind(fn)` captures the current context into a function so it runs with the right store later. Also keep stores small and never cache them globally — they hold references for as long as the async flow lives.

Under the hood, Node 22 builds this on **async_hooks** (`createHook` with `init`/`before`/`after` callbacks for every async resource), plus promise hooks. That low-level API is costly and its hook-based parts are discouraged for application code; use `AsyncLocalStorage` instead. Node 22 also offers `--experimental-async-context-frame` (the default from Node 24), which stores context in V8's continuation-preserved embedder data and makes propagation much cheaper.
takeaways: `als.run(store, fn)` scopes a store to everything `fn` starts asynchronously
`getStore()` reads it anywhere below — ideal for request IDs and tracing
Use `bind` when a library runs your callback from a shared queue
Prefer AsyncLocalStorage over raw async_hooks
pitfalls: Storing the current request in a module-level variable, which leaks between concurrent requests.

quiz.q: Two requests interleave across awaits. Why does AsyncLocalStorage return the right requestId for each?
options: The store is attached to each async flow and propagates through awaits and callbacks it creates
It locks the event loop per request
It stores data in thread-local storage on separate threads
It reads the ID from the socket each time
quiz.explain: Context follows the async continuation chain created inside run(), not the global execution order.

concepts.name: diagnostics_channel and tracing
concepts.summary: Publish and subscribe to named diagnostic events with diagnostics_channel and TracingChannel, the hooks APM tools use.
concepts.why: It is how modern Node and libraries expose observability without monkey-patching.
concepts.body:
APM and tracing tools used to **monkey-patch** library internals to measure them — fragile and version-dependent. **`node:diagnostics_channel`** replaces that with an explicit publish/subscribe bus for diagnostic data.

- A library creates a named channel, `dc.channel("mylib:query")`, and calls `channel.publish(message)` at interesting points.
- A tool calls `dc.subscribe("mylib:query", handler)` to receive those messages.
- `channel.hasSubscribers` is false when nobody listens, so the library can skip building messages entirely; publishing with no subscribers is essentially free.

Name channels with a module prefix (`undici:request:create`, `mylib:query`) to avoid collisions. Subscribers run **synchronously** inside `publish`, so they must be fast and must not throw — exceptions are reported as uncaught but don't break the publisher.

For operations with a start and an end, **`TracingChannel`** standardises five channels — `start`, `end`, `asyncStart`, `asyncEnd`, `error` — and helpers that wrap a function: `tracingChannel.tracePromise(fn, context)` publishes them around a promise-returning call. The same mutable `context` object flows through all events, so a subscriber can store a start time in `start` and compute duration in `asyncEnd`.

Node core already publishes: `http.client.request.start`, `http.server.request.start`, `net` socket events, `worker_threads` creation, and **undici** (the engine behind `fetch`) publishes request lifecycle channels. OpenTelemetry instrumentations increasingly subscribe here.

Combine it with **AsyncLocalStorage**: `channel.bindStore(als, transform)` sets a store when the channel's events run, so spans become the active context for code inside.

If you author a library, adding a few channels is a cheap, high-value way to make it observable.
takeaways: Libraries publish to named channels; tools subscribe — no monkey-patching
Publishing without subscribers is nearly free; check `hasSubscribers` before building messages
TracingChannel standardises start/end/asyncStart/asyncEnd/error with a shared context
Node core and undici already publish channels
pitfalls: Doing slow work or throwing inside a subscriber, which runs synchronously in the publisher's path.

quiz.q: What problem does diagnostics_channel primarily solve?
options: Letting tools observe library internals through explicit events instead of monkey-patching
quiz.explain: It is a low-overhead pub/sub designed specifically for diagnostics and instrumentation.

concepts.name: Graceful shutdown and production lifecycle
concepts.summary: Shut down without dropping requests: handle signals, drain keep-alive connections, close resources in order, and add health checks.
concepts.why: Every deploy and autoscaling event stops processes; done badly, users see errors every time.
concepts.body:
Orchestrators stop a process by sending **SIGTERM**, waiting a grace period (30 s by default in Kubernetes), then sending **SIGKILL**. A graceful shutdown uses that window to finish in-flight work.

The sequence:

- **Stop receiving traffic.** Flip your readiness check to failing so the load balancer drains you. In Kubernetes, endpoint removal is asynchronous, so a short delay before closing the listener avoids refused connections.
- **Stop accepting connections**: `server.close(callback)`. It stops listening and (since Node 19) also closes idle keep-alive sockets, but the callback fires only when *every* connection has ended — requests in progress, slow uploads, SSE streams and WebSockets keep it waiting.
- **Drain connections.** Let in-flight requests finish; tell long-lived streams to wind down. After a deadline, `server.closeAllConnections()` forcibly closes whatever is left.
- **Finish background work** — queues, timers, pending writes — and **close resources** in reverse order of creation: HTTP server, then job consumers, then database pools, then flush logs.
- **Exit** with a timer as a safety net: `setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10_000).unref()`. `unref()` means the timer itself doesn't keep the process alive.

Watch out for the process being **PID 1** in a container: without a handler Node won't get default signal behaviour there, and `npm start` as the entrypoint may not forward signals at all. Run `node` directly (`CMD ["node", "server.js"]`) or use an init like `tini`.

Track open handles with `ref`/`unref`: anything that keeps the loop alive (intervals, sockets) prevents natural exit; `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` lists them when shutdown hangs.

Make shutdown idempotent — SIGTERM and SIGINT may both arrive — and test it by sending signals under load.
takeaways: SIGTERM → fail readiness → close server → drain connections → close resources → exit
`server.close` waits for active connections; force stragglers with `closeAllConnections`
Use an unref'd timer as a forced-exit safety net
Run node directly (or under tini) so it receives signals in containers
pitfalls: Using `npm start` as the container command so SIGTERM never reaches Node.
Calling `process.exit()` immediately on SIGTERM and cutting off in-flight requests.

quiz.q: During shutdown, server.close()'s callback hasn't fired after 30 seconds. Most likely reason?
options: The port is still bound by the OS
A long-lived connection such as an SSE stream or WebSocket is still open
close() requires a SIGKILL to complete
The event loop is stuck in the check phase
quiz.explain: close() waits for every open connection to end; long-lived streams must be ended or force-closed with closeAllConnections().

quiz.q: Why call .unref() on the forced-exit timer?
options: So it doesn't by itself keep the process alive if shutdown finishes
To make it run on another thread
quiz.explain: An unref'd timer still fires if the process is alive, but won't prevent a natural exit.
